summary:
SaberTech is a 3D first-person interactive simulator developed in Godot 4.7 that allows players to design, launch, and operate a crewed space mission to the Moon.

The game addresses the challenge of competing engineering demands through a realistic simulation system: players assemble their spacecraft by managing five critical variables in real time—budget, mass, power, data rate, and delta-v—facing direct consequences such as structural failures or launch explosions. During the eight-turn orbital transit, players walk through the ship's modules (cockpit, living quarters, and airlock), manage power consumption, handle random events, and monitor the crew's physical and mental health against effects like low sanity. The mission culminates in a lunar landing and planting the flag on the Moon's surface.

This project is important because it transforms complex, abstract aerospace engineering concepts into an accessible, immersive, and engaging experience, allowing students to experiment with the real-world trade-offs of a space mission.
details:
What does it do and how does it work SaberTech is a first-person space simulator that guides players through the five phases of a crewed lunar mission: Briefing, Design, Launch, Orbital Operations, and Final Report. During the design phase, users assemble a modular spacecraft by selecting rockets, engines, solar panels, antennas, scientific instruments, and shielding while monitoring five real-time engineering gauges: budget, total mass, power, data transmission rate, and delta-v (calculated via the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation). Flawed designs trigger realistic physical failures during the launch cinematic, such as failing to lift off due to excess mass or mid-flight explosions caused by low reliability. Once in orbit, players walk in first person through the ship modules (cockpit, living quarters, and airlock), manage power distribution across 8 turns, resolve random space hazards (such as Van Allen belts or micrometeoroid showers), monitor crew health, and ultimately land on the Moon to walk under lunar gravity and plant the flag.

What tools, programming languages, and software did you use

  • Engine and Programming: Godot Engine using GDScript with a decoupled architecture based on Autoload singletons and signals (GameState, Estilo, Idioma, Alucinaciones), driven by data-balanced JSON configurations (datos.json).
  • 3D Modeling and Automation: Blender, utilizing procedural Python scripts to automatically generate beveled meshes, weighted normals, and modular attachment points exported as glb assets.
  • Graphics and Shaders: Custom shaders (retro.gdshader, contornos.gdshader, material_retro.gdshader) paired with modern lighting (SSAO, SSIL, SSR, volumetric fog, and filmic tonemapping), plus Python scripts for procedural texture generation.
  • Localization and Testing: Built-in bilingual support (Spanish and English) using translation catalogs and Python validation scripts, alongside automated headless test scenes.

How is your project creative

  • N64 with Modern Lighting Aesthetic: We blended the nostalgic low-poly geometry and ordered color dithering of the Nintendo 64 era with modern global illumination, dark outlines, and real-time screen-space reflections.
  • Sanity and Hallucination Mechanics: Beyond pure engineering, we modeled the psychological toll of spaceflight. If the crew skips rest in the living quarters or faces high stress, sanity drops, triggering visual wave distortions, fake Mission Control transmissions, and fleeting phantom astronaut echoes.
  • Diegetic Immersion: Management interfaces are integrated directly into the cockpit physical consoles, while ship viewports dynamically display the launchpad, orbital transit, or the lunar surface.

What factors did the team take into account We focused on balancing scientific rigor (orbital mechanics, thermal management, data memory limits, and solar power drop-off) with approachable gameplay so students would not feel overwhelmed. We also factored in language accessibility (instant switching between English and Spanish) and a modular, data-driven architecture that allowed our team to iterate rapidly within the hackathon timeframe.

Benefits and Expected Impact SaberTech removes the abstract barrier of aerospace engineering, turning it into a hands-on interactive sandbox where experimentation and failure drive learning. Its expected impact is to inspire STEM curiosity and help students intuitively grasp how trade-offs in cost, mass, power, and human factors dictate the success of a real-world space mission.
